calorias.texto: It starts with your expenditure: the Mifflin-St Jeor formula, with your height, weight, age and activity. Each week, the check-in compares what you ate with how your trend changed, and adjusts it little by little. Your goal is that expenditure, minus (or plus) what your pace asks for: each kilo is about 7,700 kcal.

macros.texto: Protein goes by body weight: 2 g per kilo when losing, 1.6 maintaining and 1.8 gaining. Fat is at least 27 % of calories and 0.6 g per kilo. Carbs are what's left, unless you choose another split.

peso.texto: Moss looks at the trend, not a single day's number: it averages your weigh-ins, so water doesn't move it as much. Your pace comes from your last six weeks, with a margin: with only a few, it's too early to tell.

grasa.texto: With a tape, using the US Navy method. That's why it's a range: against a lab scan, it can be off by about 4 points or more.

sueno.texto: With a watch or a ring, what comes through Health. Without them, Moss looks at your phone's last activity at night and first in the morning, and counts how long you take to fall asleep, which it learns from your answers.

alimentos.texto: Official tables: USDA and, for the most common foods, a second table to verify; chains, with their own. Anything marked “approximate” is an estimate, and you can fix it.

como.cinturaHombre: Level with your navel, standing, belly relaxed. Measure at the end of a normal breath out, without sucking in.
como.cinturaMujer: At the narrowest point, between your navel and breastbone. If it isn’t clear, measure a few times and keep the smallest.
como.cuello: Just below the Adam’s apple, tape straight around the neck, chin forward, shoulders down. Snug: self-measured necks tend to read large.
como.cadera: At the widest part of your buttocks, seen from the side, feet together.
como.brazo: Halfway between the tip of your shoulder and your elbow, arm relaxed at your side.
como.pecho: At the middle of your breastbone, tape under your arms, after breathing out.
como.muslo: Halfway between the crease of your groin and the top of your kneecap.

consejos: A tape that doesn’t stretch, on bare skin.
Standing, feet together, arms at your sides, relaxed.
Keep the tape level with the floor: a mirror helps.
At the end of a normal breath out: don’t suck in.
Always at the same time of day, before eating and after the bathroom.
Measure twice; if they differ by more than 1 cm, a third time, and write down the average.
cuerpo.usaHombre: The estimate uses your waist and neck, with your height. The other measurements help you follow your progress.
cuerpo.usaMujer: The estimate uses your waist, hips and neck, with your height. The other measurements help you follow your progress.
cuerpo.aviso: This is an estimate from your measurements, not a measurement: a lab scan (DEXA) could read about 4 points higher or lower, sometimes more. Over a few weeks the tape may miss a change in fat, especially in women: your waist shows it better. It’s less precise with very little fat, a lot of muscle or a lot of fat, and it doesn’t apply during pregnancy or under 18. Measure the same way every time and watch the trend.
cuerpo.comoSeEstimaHombre: With the US Navy method (Hodgdon and Beckett, 1984): body density comes from your waist minus your neck and your height, and body fat from the Siri equation. The range is the estimate plus and minus how much it changes if the tape shifts 1 cm at the waist and half a centimetre at the neck, rounded to whole points. With very little or a lot of fat, it opens one more point on each side.
cuerpo.comoSeEstimaMujer: With the US Navy method (Hodgdon and Beckett, 1984): body density comes from your waist plus your hips minus your neck and your height, and body fat from the Siri equation. The range is the estimate plus and minus how much it changes if the tape shifts 1 cm at the waist and hips and half a centimetre at the neck, rounded to whole points. With very little or a lot of fat, it opens one more point on each side.

comoCalidad: It’s a Moss number, from 0 to 100, in three parts. It isn’t Apple’s Sleep Score: Apple doesn’t share it with other apps, so they may not match.
Duration (50): how long you slept against what you need ({necesidad}). 4 hours scores 0, and reaching it scores 50.

Timing (30): how far your sleep and wake times moved from your usual ones (the median of your last two weeks). Up to half an hour scores everything; an hour and a half or more, nothing. With fewer than 5 nights it’s left out and the total is rescaled.
Continuity (20): minutes awake between falling asleep and waking up (full up to 20, none from 60) and awakenings of 5 minutes or more (full with one, none with four).
Stages, time in bed and heart rate aren’t included: the watch measures them less accurately.
sueno.regularidadTexto: From {n} of the last 14 nights. The ± is how much your time moves from night to night: up to half an hour is very regular. The weekend compares the middle of your Friday and Saturday nights with the rest, assuming you don’t work those days.
sueno.deudaDe: short of what you need ({necesidad} a night)
sueno.deudaTexto: What you were short of what you need each night over the last two weeks, counting recent nights more, minus what you slept extra (up to 2 hours a night). Naps count. It's worked out from the nights with data, so missing nights don't lower it. It's approximate: it depends mostly on how much sleep you need.
sueno.vitalesTexto: The average while you slept, against the median of your previous nights (7 are needed). The watch measures variability only a few times a night: it’s the least precise. Resting heart rate is for the whole day.
sueno.fuentesTexto: Moss uses a single source per night: the one you choose in Profile › Devices or, if not, the one that best tells sleep from wake. It never adds two together. Without a watch or a ring, it estimates the night with your phone. If a night is missing, it stays grey: nothing is made up.
sueno.noMedico: Moss isn’t a medical device. If you’re worried about your sleep, talk to a doctor.

privacidadTexto: Your data is yours. Moss stores what you log, your answers, your weight and your nights on your phone and, with your account, on its server, for your other devices. It doesn't sell them or share them with third parties, show ads or track you.

From Apple Health, Moss reads steps, sleep, water, mindful minutes, weight, date of birth, sex and height and, at night, heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability and respiratory rate. With your account, your weight, birth year, sex, height, which habits you completed and the estimated time of your night are uploaded; everything else stays on your phone. Moss never writes to Apple Health.
Meal photos and your profile photo stay on your phone. When you scan a code that isn't in Moss, Open Food Facts is asked about that code only.
If you choose to, what you search for and don't find is sent without your name; so is a mistake you report. You can export everything as CSV and delete your data or your account here.

perfil.calidadTexto: If anything stutters, Automatic steps down by itself. Low uses less battery.
perfil.corteTexto: Anything you log before that time counts for the day before: if you eat dinner or go to bed late, it's still your day.

aparatos.varios: If you use more than one, Moss takes one per night, the one you choose, and never adds them together.

iphone.texto: With just the iPhone, Moss estimates when you slept from your steps, your phone’s motion and when you use the app, and asks you in the morning to confirm it. With a watch or a ring, it’s measured.

appleWatch.texto: How long and when you slept, with stages and naps; at night, your heart rate, heart rate variability and breathing; wrist temperature from Series 8 on, and blood oxygen on the models that measure it.

oura.texto: How long and when you slept, with stages, and the night’s heart rate and breathing. Variability and temperature stay in the Oura app. Open it every day so the data comes through.

whoop.texto: How long and when you slept, without stages, and the night’s resting heart rate, breathing and blood oxygen. Stages and variability stay in the WHOOP app.

garmin.texto: How long and when you slept, with stages, your heart rate and steps. Open Garmin Connect so it sends the data. Variability and Body Battery stay in Garmin.

google.texto: With a Fitbit or a Fitbit Air: how long and when you slept, with stages, heart rate, resting heart rate, breathing and blood oxygen. Connect the Google Health app to Health. Variability doesn’t come through.

polar.texto: How long you slept, without stages, your steps and workouts.

withings.texto: Your weight and body composition; with the Sleep Analyzer or a ScanWatch, your sleep too. If you created your account after October 12, 2026, you need Withings+ to send data to Health.

avisos.tardoTexto: From when you put your phone down until you fall asleep. Moss learns it every time you answer “Did you sleep from… to…?”.
avisos.maximoTexto: Moss never reminds you more times than this in one day. If there are more, bedtime and your habits come first.
avisos.horarioTexto: A reminder at each meal time, to keep your meals on schedule. If you already logged it, it stays quiet; with a plan, it says what’s next.
avisos.pesarseTexto: Shortly after you wake up, after the bathroom and before breakfast: the trend comes from weighing the same way. If you already weighed in, it stays quiet.

baseInfo.intro: No number in Moss comes out of a black box: they're published formulas, guidelines from scientific societies and what you log or your watch measures. Here's where each one comes from and how much you can trust it.
baseInfo.comoTitulo: How we organize what comes in
reglas: What's measured comes before what's estimated, and estimates say "approx."
Without data, Moss doesn't make things up: it tells you what's missing.
Your day starts at the time you choose (4 a.m. by default): the small hours belong to the night before.
Everything stays on your phone first; with your account, in the cloud too, the same on your other phones.

sueno.texto: For sleep, Moss follows the recommendations of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society (2015), which advise adults to sleep 7 hours or more, and those of the National Sleep Foundation (2015 and 2017), which set the ranges for each age and what counts as continuous sleep. With a watch or a ring, Moss relies mostly on how long and when you slept, which is what these devices measure best: in studies against polysomnography they detect more than 90% of sleep but miss much of the time spent awake, and sleep stages are much less accurate (Schyvens et al., 2025). The regularity of your schedule matters because, in large studies, it is linked to health, sometimes more strongly than duration (Windred et al., 2024). Quality, sleep debt and regularity are estimates for seeing trends, not diagnoses: debt depends mostly on how much sleep you need, which varies from person to person, and without a watch Moss estimates your night from your phone and asks you to confirm or correct it.
sueno.fuentes: AASM and SRS, 2015 · National Sleep Foundation, 2015 and 2017 · Schyvens et al., 2025 · Windred et al., 2024

momentos.texto: The notifications that tell you when to stop caffeine, when to have your last big meal, how late to train hard and when to dim the lights come from reviews of studies and expert consensus. The caffeine cutoff follows the meta-analysis by Gardiner and colleagues (2023), which estimated how many hours before bed caffeine stops costing you sleep depending on the dose; the lighting advice follows a consensus of 18 light and sleep experts led by Brown (2022); and eating around training follows the meta-analysis by King and colleagues (2022) for strength and the American College of Sports Medicine position (2016) for endurance. Moss counts each time back from your bedtime and your training, so treat it as an approximate guide: people respond differently, especially to caffeine and alcohol. This is advice for healthy people; if you have slept badly for months, what helps most is cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, and it is worth talking to a doctor.
momentos.fuentes: Gardiner et al., 2023 · Brown et al., 2022 · King et al., 2022 · American College of Sports Medicine, 2016

fotos.titulo: Why we don't calculate your food from a photo
fotos.texto: A photo shows what's on the plate, but not how much it weighs or what you can't see, like oil, butter or a filling. In 52 photos of weighed meals, three general-purpose AIs missed the calories by 36% to 64% on average, and by more on larger plates (Fridolfsson and colleagues, 2025); another AI, trained on thousands of meals, nearly tripled its error when it also had to guess the portion (Thames and colleagues, 2021). That's why in Moss you pick the food from a reviewed database, scan the barcode or the label, or say what you ate, and Moss asks about what a photo can't see, like the oil. It isn't exact either: a label can be up to 20% off (Mercosur and EU rules allow it), and anything estimated by eye has its margin. But you can narrow that error by weighing or choosing the portion, and if it repeats in a similar way, the weekly check-in makes up for it with your weight.
fotos.fuentes: Fridolfsson and colleagues, 2025 · Thames and colleagues, 2021 · Mercosur, RDC 360/2003

ascent.texto: The Ascent section combines your sets from Ascent with your sleep and food, and relies on the strongest research available. Sleeping 6 hours or less lowers maximal strength only a little but reduces repetitions much more (Craven et al., 2022, pooling 77 studies); your strength also varies by about 3–5% from one day to the next for no particular reason (Grgic et al., 2020), and doing more sets per week brings more progress, though with diminishing returns (Pelland et al., 2026). Because the validity of wearable “recovery” scores hasn't been shown (Doherty et al., 2025), Moss doesn't give you a percentage: it shows your data, tells you when something is out of the ordinary, and says when there isn't enough data yet to know. It's guidance, not a diagnosis.
ascent.fuentes: Craven et al., 2022 · Grgic et al., 2020 · Pelland et al., 2026 · Doherty et al., 2025

metas.texto: To start, Moss estimates how much energy you use with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (1990), the most accurate one for adults, and adds your daily activity and training following the US National Academies (2023): it is a starting point that can be off by 10% or more, not your exact number. Then, every week, it compares what you log with your weight trend and corrects the estimate; measuring energy balance from repeated weigh-ins has been checked against laboratory methods (Sanghvi, Hall and colleagues, 2015), and after three or four weeks of frequent weigh-ins the number becomes solid. Protein follows the meta-analysis by Morton and colleagues (2018), 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg if you train and never below 1.2, while fats, fiber and vitamins follow the National Academies' references. These are guidelines for healthy adults, not a diagnosis: if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or have a medical condition, Moss won't put you in a deficit and suggests talking to a professional.
metas.fuentes: Mifflin et al., 1990 · National Academies (NASEM), 2023 · Sanghvi et al., 2015 · Morton et al., 2018

progreso.texto: Your weight goes up and down from day to day with water, what you ate the day before and, in women, the menstrual cycle, so Moss doesn't go by a single day's number: it follows the trend of your weigh-ins and calculates your rate over the last few weeks with a margin, because with only a few weeks of data it is still uncertain (Hall and Chow, 2011). The rates it suggests never go above 1% of your body weight per week, the range research uses to lose fat while protecting muscle (Helms et al., 2014), and it never accepts a goal weight below a body mass index of 18.5, the WHO threshold. Body fat from a tape measure uses the U.S. Navy formula: it is an estimate that can differ by about 4 points or more from a lab scan (Foulis et al., 2023), so take it as a guide. To see how your body is changing, watch your waist: the NICE guideline (2025) recommends keeping it under half your height.
progreso.fuentes: Hall and Chow, 2011 · Helms et al., 2014 · WHO · Foulis et al., 2023 · NICE, 2025

cuidados.texto: If you mark a health condition, Moss adjusts your targets to guidelines for the general population and stops suggesting things that may not suit you, like eating less or pushing protein up. For pregnancy and breastfeeding it uses the US National Academies' references (2023) and the IOM's weight-gain ranges (2009); for diabetes, the American Diabetes Association's (2026); and for kidneys, KDIGO's (2024). These changes are general and approximate: they don't replace what your healthcare team tells you, and you can always enter the targets they give you. What you mark is stored only on this iPhone.
cuidados.fuentes: NASEM, 2023 · IOM, 2009 · ADA, 2026 · KDIGO, 2024 · EAU, 2026 · ESC/EAS, 2019 · WHO

base.porcentaje: Why there's no percentage: no recovery score from watches or rings has been validated against performance (Doherty 2025), and a sum compensates: with nights of 4.5 to 6 hours, it almost always said “good”. So the weakest link decides, and you see your data.
base.titular: The headline: first, what changes today's session. What you train, if it's still loaded; your night, if it was 6 hours or less, if you woke up an hour early or if two of your last three were short (Craven 2022; Kong 2025; Knowles 2018); and how you say you feel, from 0 to 10 (Laurent 2011).
base.noche: A short night: maximal strength barely changes and reps may feel harder (across 77 studies, −3% and −10%: Craven 2022). Not going to failure is enough: you don't need it to gain strength (Grgic 2022). Night quality is shown but doesn't count: almost no study measured it.
base.musculos: Your muscles: from your sets in Ascent, each muscle as the main one or as a helper, and how long it takes to come back, longer for legs and with more sets (Belcher 2019; Bartolomei 2017). It's said in days because it can be off by one, and soreness doesn't count: strength comes back sooner (Soares 2015).
base.fuerza: Your strength: each exercise's 12-week trend, with the estimated 1RM of your best set each session and its 80% range. Strength varies ~3% from day to day for no reason (Grgic 2020): with fewer weeks or sessions, it's too early to tell.
base.marca: Personal bests: close means your level today (the trend) is within how much your strength varies from day to day. No probability: no study predicts the day of a best, and saying how often you hit one is more accurate.
base.estancamiento: Plateaus: 8 weeks with no clear increase, past Ascent's threshold. The reasons go from most to least solid: hard sets per week (Pelland 2026), how often, heavy loads (Lopez 2021; ACSM 2026), losing weight fast (Garthe 2011), protein against 1.6 g per kilo (Morton 2018) and sleep. It's always a probable cause, not a sure one.
base.comer: Food: about 1 g of carbs per kilo before a long session (King 2022) and 20 to 40 g of protein per meal. Coffee, about 9 hours before bed with one coffee and 13 with a pre-workout (Gardiner 2023); hard training, ideally 4 hours before bed and at least 2 (Frimpong 2021; Leota 2025).

porQue.antes: Before a long session, carbs in the hours before help you perform; close to training, keep it light so it sits well. For a short session, your usual meal is enough.
porQue.despues: What matters most is protein across the whole day, spread over your meals. After training, about 0.3 g per kilo in the next meal helps recovery; no need to rush unless it has been many hours without food.
porQue.reponer: With two sessions on the same day, carbs in between help you start the second one with energy.
porQue.antesDeDormir: Protein before bed counts toward the day too: 30 to 40 g, for example from yogurt or milk.
porQue.cafeina: Caffeine takes hours to clear: late in the day, it makes sleep shallower even if you still fall asleep.
porQue.fuentes: Sources: King et al. (2022), for strength; ACSM, Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Dietitians of Canada (2016), for endurance; ISSN, Kerksick et al. (2017) and Jäger et al. (2017); Morton et al. (2018); Schoenfeld and Aragon (2018); Gardiner et al. (2023).
porQue.medico: This is general guidance for healthy people. It is not medical advice.
porQue.volver: You can turn it back on in Profile › Training.
porQue.nocheCorta: Sleeping too little makes you hungrier: in studies, people eat about 200 to 385 more kcal that day. It’s normal, and there’s nothing to make up for: your target doesn’t change.
porQue.fuentesNocheCorta: Sources: Al Khatib et al. (2017); Fenton et al. (2021); Zhu et al. (2019).

lineas.embarazo: During pregnancy, Moss won't suggest losing weight, adds what the second and third trimesters need and pauses the weekly check-in. Your healthcare team follows your weight with you.
lineas.lactancia: While you breastfeed, Moss adds about 400 kcal a day. If you want to lose weight, start after the first month and go slowly.
lineas.diabetes2: Eating a varied diet and, if you need to, losing a little weight may help you live well with type 2 diabetes. If you take insulin or another glucose-lowering medicine, talk to your healthcare team before eating less.
lineas.diabetes1: Moss shows you the carbs in each meal, but it doesn't calculate insulin or tell you what to eat around exercise: that's for you and your healthcare team.
lineas.presion: With high blood pressure, Moss shows you the salt and potassium in what you eat. Eating less salt and, if you need to, losing weight may help you live well with high blood pressure.
lineas.colesterol: Moss shows you the saturated fat and fiber in what you eat. If your doctor gave you other targets, you can enter them yourself.
lineas.renal: With kidney disease, Moss doesn't push protein up: it stays at 0.8 g per kilo, as KDIGO recommends. It shows you the salt, and it won't ask you to eat less or drink more water. Your healthcare team decides the rest.
lineas.calculos: With kidney stones, drinking water is the top recommendation: Moss sets a goal of 2.5 to 3 liters a day and shows you the salt.
lineas.reflujo: With reflux, Moss reminds you to finish eating about 3 hours before bed.
lineas.celiaquia: With celiac disease, your plan and Moss's ideas skip wheat, barley, rye and oats. Moss can't tell whether a product has gluten: check for a certified gluten-free label.
lineas.gota: With gout, Moss shows you the alcohol and sugary drinks in what you log.
lineas.tca: Moss won't suggest eating less, can hide the numbers and won't nudge you about eating more or less. If you're in treatment, use Moss only if your team agrees.
lineas.glp1: With your medication, Moss helps you reach your protein and suggests smaller meals; your healthcare team follows your treatment.
lineas.otra: Moss won't suggest eating less than you burn or push more protein or water. If your healthcare team gives you targets, you can enter them yourself.
